extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media scholars, and students of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative principles for judging the quality, reliability, and social function of news reporting and editorial selection in a modern press system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for apparatus and rules for naming, scoring, recording
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purposes of newsgathering it is impossible to do much without an apparatus and rules for naming, scoring, recording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because that machinery is far from perfect the umpire's life is often a distracted one; many crucial plays must be judged by eye. When there is good machinery of record (e.g., moving pictures in boxing) disputes can be settled; without it reporters and editors must rely on imperfect observation and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between certainty of news and system of record
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a very direct relation between the certainty of news and the system of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics with dependable record systems (stock exchange tickers, election returns, births/deaths, imports/exports) yield precise news. Where records are scarce or informal (internal trade, over-the-counter trade, many aspects of industry and government), news is much less certain and more disputable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited reportability of states of mind and intangible facts
rubrics_metrics.description: News about states of mind, personalities, sincerity, motive, intention, mass feeling, public opinion, and much about what is going to happen are of a character where the data are at best spasmodically recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such subjects are inherently debatable or neglected because data may be hidden (censorship, privacy), not recorded, or lack objective measurement; consequently reporting on them is often contestable and opinionated rather than definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events not scored become news only when someone makes an issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Events which are not scored are reported either as personal and conventional opinions, or they are not news; they do not take shape until somebody protests, investigates, or publicly makes an issue of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the role of press agents and interest groups in shaping what becomes news: without an overt act or publicizing, many matters remain invisible to routine journalistic reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence and role of the press/publicity agent
rubrics_metrics.description: The publicity (press) agent stands between organized groups and newspapers and selects the picture of a situation he wishes the public to see; he is censor and propagandist, responsible primarily to his employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reporters cannot always shape facts by themselves and because facts are often shapeless, organized groups employ press agents who may arrange stunts or events to make their cause newsworthy; this both aids reporters and introduces bias toward employers' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: News typically requires an overt signal (stunt, demand, disorder)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news is an account of the overt phases that are interesting; underlying conditions become reportable mainly when signaled by overt acts such as a demand, a strike, or disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and readers often see only the overt act and familiar stereotypes. Deep, complex causes (e.g., conditions producing a strike) are difficult to report without expensive investigation; thus routine reporting emphasizes the signal rather than the underlying issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints shape news selection (cost, time, talent, space)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations and in-depth reporting cost time, money, special talent, and space; newspapers cannot normally undertake extensive inquiries for many stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make plausible a major report often requires many columns, staffs of investigators, and long-term projects (e.g., Pittsburgh Surveys). Daily papers operate under strict deadlines, page limits, libel risk, and competition for attention, which favor standardized, rapid reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stereotypes and conventions to secure reader identification
rubrics_metrics.description: To interest readers quickly newspapers use stereotypes and conventions so readers can identify personally with distant facts and 'enter into' the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotypes (e.g., labeling a group a 'combine' vs 'leading business men') cue readers how to feel. This provokes identification, makes complex matters immediately graspable, but also channels interpretation and can distort nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor’s selection and the preference for indisputable facts and reader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Every newspaper is the result of selections about what to print, position, space, emphasis; editors naturally prefer indisputable facts and treatments adapted to perceived reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors work under the pressure of competing newspapers, tight deadlines, and a need to 'woo' readers; they must make swift judgments and often 'play up' or 'play down' items for probable public interest rather than for comprehensive truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility to judge and report source reliability accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and newspapers are most responsible in their judgment of the reliability of sources; they must avoid making a claim stronger than their source warrants (e.g., not asserting 'Lenin dead' when the paper only has an unreliable report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The news headline should reflect the degree of source reliability ('Helsingfors says Lenin is dead') rather than amplifying unverified claims. Proper attribution and restraint are required where objective tests do not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between news and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: News and truth are not the same thing; the function of news is to signalize an event, the function of truth is to bring to light the hidden facts and set them into relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only where social conditions are measurable and recorded do news and truth coincide. Expecting newspapers to supply the whole body of truth is a misplaced standard; news typically conveys signals, not comprehensive truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the press as a substitute for institutions and organized intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is no substitute for institutions; the quality of news about modern society is an index of social organization and the existence of formal representation and objective criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better institutions, transparent representation, and comparable records enable more objective news. Conversely, where institutions fail to record and analyze, the press cannot reliably supply the missing knowledge and may be exploited by unscrupulous actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for specialized experts and methods to extend reportable truth
rubrics_metrics.description: To extend the body of reportable truth there must be organized intelligence: statisticians, auditors, industrial counselors, engineers, research men — specialists who make parts of society intelligible through records and quantitative analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specialists bring filing systems, card catalogues, graphs, and a technic of presenting policy matters in a form ready for decisions. The press can prod social science and statesmen to create such instruments, but cannot itself usually generate them.
